title: What is known about 1RB1RC_1LC0RE_1LD0LB_1RA1LC_1RA1RF_---1RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RC_1LC0RE_1LD0LB_1RA1LC_1RA1RF_---1RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, but the machine is now well understood. Behind a block of 1s that grows by two each sweep sits a chain of small counters that each count 0, 1, 2, 3, followed by a chaotic tail. The chain is exactly predictable, so the run was followed, with exact step counts, through 2.80·1036 sweeps (2.35·1073 steps): no halt, and the third event turned the block into a chain of 4.67·1035 counters. Lean proves that the machine can only halt on the blank tape beyond the far end, which the head will not see again for more than (4/3)4.67·10^35 sweeps. Whether that contact, or a later one, halts depends on the chaotic tail.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 39,306 cells have been visited and 26,537 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: A halt can only happen beyond the far end
claims.text: Every configuration of the run from blank tape lies in a closed tape language (windows of six cells on each side of the head plus the parity of the distance to the next 0; 5,545 abstract configurations). In it, the halting transition can only fire with blank tape from the head on. So the machine halts if and only if F steps onto the blank tape right of everything.

claims.title: The region is a chain of mod-4 counters and a tail
claims.text: At each visit of the left end in state D the tape is D>0 1^n R; in pairs a = 01, b = 11, R = aaa S[s_0] ... S[s_m-1] junk with S = [baabaa, abbabb, bbbbbb, aaaaaa]. A double visit adds 1 to s_0 and goes on to the next counter unless the counter was 0; the junk changes only at sweeps that pass the whole chain, by a map of its own (3,000 recorded passes replayed behind four different chains). The reference implementation agrees with the direct run at every visit up to 6,000 (step count, block, region), through two events.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2.35·10<sup>73</sup> steps; the third event
claims.text: Events after visits 3, 13, 23, 97 and 1,481. The exact accelerated run (closed-form jumps over the sweeps that turn inside the chain, cell-by-cell passes; 128-bit visits, 256-bit steps) follows epoch 3 through 25,741,416 passes of its 230 counters. The next event is in the double visit after visit 2,802,669,362,130,569,848,949,782,677,328,552,882; the following visit, 2,802,669,472,598,490,952,316,788,103,359,480,650, has block 12, comes at step 23,564,868,517,906,510,281,033,392,402,285,525,944,194,469,908,788,408,626,361,071,990,157,929,983, and its region is 2,802,669,472,598,490,952,316,788,103,359,479,170 pairs 01 followed by a 2,985-cell tail.

claims.title: The next contact: more than (4/3)<sup>4.67·10^35</sup> sweeps away
claims.text: A sweep passes a chain of m counters once in about (4/3)m double visits (exact formula in jump); the new chain has 4.67·1035 counters, and the 221-cell junk of epoch 3 needed 2.6·107 passes before the event.

claims.title: In short-block models every run halts, at the far end
claims.text: The real machine with the block cut back to 4 cells at every visit, from random regions of 8 pairs: all of 2,000 runs halt within 12 events, with blank tape right of the head. With the last 21 or 41 cells of the true tail of epoch 4 at the far end, none of 400 runs halts at the first contact.

claims.title: Growth shape: fixed/sqrt
claims.text: The head sweeps across the whole tape and adds two cells per sweep at the left end, so the tape grows like the square root of the step count.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. It comes down to the junk: an autonomous map on a few thousand cells, applied once per pass of the chain, with no regular digits found (blocks of 18, 28, 28 cells with 55, 181, 292+ states, then no pattern). Which of its far-end contacts halt is the whole question.

check: python3 holdouts/1RB1RC_1LC0RE_1LD0LB_1RA1LC_1RA1RF_---1RD/py/test_chain.py 6000   # the chain rule against the direct run
./chainrun -direct 1488 s1488.txt && ./chainrun s1488.txt 1000000000 s_end.txt   # to the third event (about 80 minutes)

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but this is the best understood machine of its family. A block of ones grows at every sweep; behind it sits a row of tiny counters, each counting 0, 1, 2, 3, and behind those a scrambled tail. The counters can be predicted exactly, which lets a computer follow the machine for 10<sup>73</sup> steps. The tail cannot. This page runs the real machine in your browser and explains the pieces.

facts.text: Proved in Lean: the machine can halt only on blank tape beyond the far end of everything it has written.
No halt: exact accelerated run to the third event, at sweep 2.80·10<sup>36</sup>.
The chain the machine has to get through before it touches the far end again.
Sweeps before the next moment at which it could halt, at least.

sections.heading: A growing block, a row of counters, a tail
html: Look at the tape each time the head reaches the left end. First a block of ones, two cells longer than last time. Behind it the cells come in pairs, 01 or 11, and groups of six pairs form little counters with four states. Behind the counters is a tail of a few thousand cells with no visible order.

<svg viewBox="0 0 580 70" role="img" aria-label="The tape: a growing uniform block, an active counter region, a more counters it eats, and an old tail at the far end" style="width:100%;max-width:620px;height:auto"><g font-family="var(--body)" font-size="11" fill="var(--fg2)"><text x="10" y="14">← grows 2 cells a sweep</text><text x="14" y="60">growing block</text><text x="184" y="60">counters</text><text x="274" y="60">more counters</text><text x="484" y="60">old tail</text></g><rect x="10" y="20" width="170" height="22" fill="var(--ink)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="180" y="20" width="90" height="22" fill="var(--heur-bg)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="270" y="20" width="210" height="22" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="480" y="20" width="90" height="22" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/></svg>
Crossing the block costs time but changes nothing, so the machine applies one fixed rule, sweep after sweep, to the part behind the block.

sections.heading: A chain of counters that count to four
html: Every second sweep adds one to the first counter. If that counter was at 0, the sweep turns around there. Otherwise it goes on and adds one to the second counter, with the same rule, and so on down the row.

<svg viewBox="0 0 580 120" role="img" aria-label="A chain of counters modulo 4: each sweep adds one to the first counter; it stops there if the counter was 0 and otherwise goes on to the next" style="width:100%;max-width:620px;height:auto"><g font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle"><rect x="40" y="30" width="52" height="30" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="66" y="50" fill="var(--fg)">2</text><rect x="100" y="30" width="52" height="30" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="126" y="50" fill="var(--fg)">3</text><rect x="160" y="30" width="52" height="30" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="186" y="50" fill="var(--fg)">1</text><rect x="220" y="30" width="52" height="30" fill="var(--heur-bg)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="246" y="50" fill="var(--fg)">0</text><rect x="280" y="30" width="52" height="30" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="306" y="50" fill="var(--fg)">3</text><rect x="340" y="30" width="52" height="30" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="366" y="50" fill="var(--fg)">2</text><rect x="400" y="30" width="150" height="30" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><text x="475" y="50" fill="var(--fg2)">junk</text></g><g font-family="var(--body)" font-size="11" fill="var(--fg2)"><text x="40" y="20">a sweep arrives from the block: +1, +1, +1, and it turns at the first counter that was 0</text><text x="40" y="100">after the sweep: 3 0 2 1 3 2 (the counters behind the turning point are untouched)</text></g><path d="M20 45 H36" stroke="var(--head)" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M66 68 q30 14 60 0 q30 14 60 0 q30 14 60 0" fill="none" stroke="var(--head)" stroke-width="1.5"/><circle cx="246" cy="68" r="3.5" fill="var(--head)"/></svg>

So three sweeps out of four get past the first counter, three out of four of those past the second, and so on: to get past a row of m counters takes about (4/3)m tries. This rule is simple enough to compute millions of sweeps in one go, with the exact number of steps: that is how the machine was followed far beyond anything a step-by-step simulation could do.

Only a sweep that gets past the whole row touches the tail, and each such pass changes the tail a little, by a rule of its own that looks chaotic. When a pass finally gets through the tail to the far end of the tape, an event happens: the whole block of ones turns into a fresh row of counters (all showing 3), the old row and tail become the new tail, and a new block starts from two cells.

Events so far: after sweeps 3, 13, 23, 97, 1,481, and then one at about sweep 2.80·1036. Between the last two, the row had 230 counters and was passed 25,741,416 times. The row that the last event created has 4.67·1035 counters.

sections.heading: Proved: only at the far end
html: The machine stops only in state F on a 0. A Lean proof shows that, starting from a blank tape, this can only happen when F steps onto the untouched blank tape beyond the far end. The proof exhibits a set of tape shapes that contains the start, is closed under the machine's steps, and contains no other halting situation. The trick was to let the shapes remember whether the head is an odd or an even number of cells from the next 0, because the machine reads its tape in pairs.
So nothing can go wrong while the head is busy with the counters or the tail. The only dangerous moments are the events, when a sweep reaches the far end.

sections.heading: A coin toss, repeated at ever longer intervals
html: Between two events nothing can go wrong: the machine sweeps, the block grows, the counter eats a little more reservoir. Everything is decided in the few sweeps in which the counter touches the far end of the tape. Each such contact either stops the machine or turns the block into the next reservoir, which is as long as the block had become, so the next contact is exponentially further away than the last one, and the one after that exponentially further again.

<svg viewBox="0 0 580 96" role="img" aria-label="Epochs: each reservoir is as long as the block was at the previous event, so each epoch is exponentially longer than the one before" style="width:100%;max-width:620px;height:auto"><g font-family="var(--body)" font-size="11" fill="var(--fg2)"><text x="10" y="14">epoch k: reservoir of L cells</text><text x="10" y="58">epoch k+1: reservoir of about 2^(L/c) cells</text><text x="300" y="36">eaten in about 2^(L/c) sweeps</text></g><rect x="10" y="20" width="60" height="18" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="70" y="20" width="14" height="18" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="10" y="64" width="520" height="18" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><rect x="530" y="64" width="14" height="18" fill="var(--sunk)" stroke="var(--line-strong)"/><circle cx="84" cy="29" r="4" fill="var(--head)"/><circle cx="544" cy="73" r="4" fill="var(--head)"/></svg>

Machines like this are called cryptids in the Busy Beaver community: their fate hangs on an unbounded sequence of yes/no questions about a pseudo-random process, and no known method answers all of them at once.

For this machine the waiting times are known rather precisely, because the counters are: the next contact needs a sweep to get past 4.67·1035 counters, about (4/3)4.67·10^35 tries, and then many such passes to work through the tail. What is not known is the one thing that matters: whether the tail, when it finally gives way, lets the machine halt. In scaled-down models (block kept at four cells) every run eventually halts.

sections.heading: What was checked, and how
html:
• The counter rule, as a program, reproduces the real machine at every one of its first 6,000 sweeps: step count, block and region, through two events.
  • The fast C version agrees with that program after 300 passes (step 3.2·1063), and its sweep numbers agree with an independent earlier program at every million passes.
  • The Lean files compile with no sorry; the large closure check uses native_decide.
  • Not known: the rule of the tail.

family: chain of mod-4 counters in front of a chaotic tail (decoded reservoir counter; cryptid-like)
summary: The reservoir is a chain of independent mod-4 counters (decoded, with an exact accelerator): the third far-end contact comes at visit 2.80e36 (step 2.35e73) and does not halt; Lean proves a halt can only happen on blank tape beyond the far end; the next contact needs more than (4/3)^(4.67e35) sweeps.
